text: A router has installed routes for 10.40.0.0/16 via A, 10.40.8.0/24 via B and 0.0.0.0/0 via C. Where does it forward a packet to 10.40.8.77?
distractors: Via A, because /16 covers more addresses
Via C, because a default route overrides specific routes
To all three next hops regardless of prefix length
explanation: Both the /16 and /24 match, but the /24 is the longest matching prefix. Forwarding selects the most specific installed route. The default route is used only when no more-specific match exists; administrative distance does not override this prefix-length comparison.

text: An IOS routing entry includes O 10.60.0.0/24 [110/20] via 192.0.2.2. What do the values in brackets represent?
distractors: Metric 110 and prefix length 20
OSPF process ID 110 and area ID 20
TCP source port 110 and destination port 20
explanation: IOS displays administrative distance followed by the route metric as [AD/metric]. O identifies an OSPF-learned route, the prefix is /24, and 192.0.2.2 is its next hop. Process and area IDs are not encoded by those bracketed values.

text: A router learns the exact same /24 prefix through an ordinary static route with administrative distance 1 and through OSPF with distance 110. Both next hops are reachable. Which source is normally preferred for installing that prefix?
correct: The static route with administrative distance 1
distractors: OSPF because dynamic information always overrides static configuration
Both routes solely because their prefix lengths match
The source with the larger administrative distance
explanation: For competing sources of the same prefix, a lower administrative distance is normally preferred. The static route wins over OSPF here. Longest-prefix forwarding applies between installed matching prefixes; it does not make all sources for one prefix equally preferred.

text: A router needs an IPv4 default static route through reachable next hop 192.0.2.1. Which IOS command expresses that route?
distractors: ip default-gateway 0.0.0.0
explanation: An IPv4 default route has prefix 0.0.0.0/0, represented by destination and mask both 0.0.0.0 in this IOS command. A /32 route is a host route. ip default-gateway is not the requested routed IPv4 default-static command, and an IPv6 route does not express this IPv4 destination.

text: An IPv6 static route should match only the single destination 2001:db8:10::7, not its surrounding subnet. What prefix length should that host route use?
explanation: An IPv6 address is 128 bits long, so a /128 route identifies exactly one address. A /64 or /48 includes many addresses; /0 is the default route. The documentation prefix in the example is for an illustrative configuration, not public deployment.

text: A reachable OSPF route to 10.70.0.0/24 has administrative distance 110. A static route through a reachable alternate next hop should install only when that OSPF route disappears. Which static administrative distance meets this requirement?
explanation: A floating static route uses a distance higher than the preferred route's distance. 200 is higher than OSPF's 110, so the OSPF route is preferred while present. A lower distance would favor the static route, and equal distance does not establish the requested strictly lower preference.

text: Two OSPFv2 routers share a broadcast subnet and use the same area and authentication. Which difference prevents their normal neighbor adjacency?
distractors: Different locally significant OSPF process IDs
Different, unique router IDs
Different host addresses within the same subnet
explanation: OSPF neighbors require compatible hello/dead intervals on the link. Process IDs are locally significant and need not match. Router IDs should be unique, and interfaces on the same subnet normally have different host addresses. Area, authentication and network parameters must also be checked during troubleshooting.

text: An OSPF broadcast segment already has a healthy DR and BDR. A new router joins with a higher interface priority than either. Without a failure or election reset, what normally happens to the current DR?
correct: It remains DR because the established election is nonpreemptive
distractors: It immediately becomes a DROTHER solely because the newcomer has higher priority
It disables its interface to prevent duplicate priorities
It switches the area to point-to-point mode
explanation: OSPF DR/BDR elections are nonpreemptive. A stronger router joining an established broadcast segment does not automatically displace the existing DR. Priority and router ID matter when an election is required, but do not by themselves force a fresh election here.

text: Two routers provide a first-hop redundancy group for a LAN. Which address should hosts generally use as their default gateway to benefit from that group?
distractors: The physical IP of whichever router was installed first
The Ethernet broadcast address
The IP address of the DNS server, regardless of its routing role
explanation: The virtual IP provides a stable gateway address while the protocol manages which router serves it. Pointing clients at one member's physical IP bypasses the intended virtual-gateway failover. DNS service and Layer 2 broadcast addresses are not substitutes for a host's IP next hop.

text: A LAN's active virtual gateway router fails. Its standby is configured to take over the same virtual IP and protocol-defined virtual MAC. What is the main benefit for correctly configured hosts?
correct: They can continue using the same default-gateway configuration after convergence
distractors: They automatically move into a different IP subnet
They no longer require a default gateway for remote destinations
Their application servers become redundant through the gateway protocol
explanation: The virtual gateway's stable IP and MAC allow the backup router to take over without manually reconfiguring each host's default gateway. Some convergence loss may occur. First-hop redundancy protects gateway availability, not arbitrary server applications or every other possible failure in the network.
